ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, both $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDE$ are equilateral triangles, with point E inside $\triangle ABC$. Line segments AE, BE, and BD are connected. If $\angle EBD=50^\circ$, what is the measure of $\angle AEB$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:}

Since $\triangle ABC$ is an equilateral triangle,

it follows that AC = BC, $\angle ACB=\angle ABC=\angle BAC=60^\circ$,

Since $\triangle CDE$ is an equilateral triangle,

it follows that CD = CE, $\angle DCE=60^\circ$

Therefore, $\angle ACB=\angle DCE$,

Therefore, $\angle ACB-\angle BCE=\angle DCE-\angle BCE$,

that is $\angle BCD=\angle ACE$,

In $\triangle ACE$ and $\triangle BCD$,

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}AC=BC\\ \angle ACE=\angle BCD\\ EC=CD\end{array}\right.$,

Therefore, $\triangle ACE \cong \triangle BCD$ (SAS),

Therefore, $\angle CAE=\angle CBD$,

Since $\angle EBD=\angle EBC+\angle CBD=50^\circ$,

Therefore, $\angle CAE+\angle EBC=50^\circ$,

Since $\angle CAB+\angle ABC=60^\circ+60^\circ=120^\circ$,

Therefore, $\angle ABE+\angle BAE=120^\circ-(\angle CAE+\angle EBC)=120^\circ-50^\circ=70^\circ$,

Therefore, $\angle AEB=180^\circ-(\angle ABE+\angle BAE)=180^\circ-70^\circ=\boxed{110^\circ}$.

raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, both $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDE$ are equilateral triangles, with point $E$ inside $\triangle ABC$. Line segments $AE$, $BE$, and $BD$ are connected. If $\angle EBD = 50^\circ$, what is the measure of $\angle AEB$?
raw_record.answer:
Solution:
Since $\triangle ABC$ is an equilateral triangle, it follows that $AC = BC$ and $\angle ACB = \angle ABC = \angle BAC = 60^\circ$.

Since $\triangle CDE$ is an equilateral triangle, it follows that $CD = CE$ and $\angle DCE = 60^\circ$.

Therefore, $\angle ACB = \angle DCE$.
Therefore, $\angle ACB - \angle BCE = \angle DCE - \angle BCE$, that is, $\angle BCD = \angle ACE$.

In $\triangle ACE$ and $\triangle BCD$,
$\left\{\begin{array}{l}AC = BC\\ \angle ACE = \angle BCD\\ EC = CD\end{array}\right.$
Therefore, $\triangle ACE \cong \triangle BCD$ (SAS).

Therefore, $\angle CAE = \angle CBD$.
Since $\angle EBD = \angle EBC + \angle CBD = 50^\circ$, therefore $\angle CAE + \angle EBC = 50^\circ$.

Since $\angle CAB + \angle ABC = 60^\circ + 60^\circ = 120^\circ$, therefore
$\angle ABE + \angle BAE = 120^\circ - (\angle CAE + \angle EBC) = 120^\circ - 50^\circ = 70^\circ$.

Therefore, $\angle AEB = 180^\circ - (\angle ABE + \angle BAE) = 180^\circ - 70^\circ = \boxed{110^\circ}$.
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, A is the upper vertex, B is on the left, C is on the right, and ABC forms an equilateral triangle; E is located inside triangle ABC, and AE, BE, CE are connected; D is located below, CDE forms another equilateral triangle, and BD is connected. What is required is the angle between EA and EB at point E, ∠AEB. Reasoning: Because △ABC is an equilateral triangle, AC = BC, and ∠ACB = ∠ABC = ∠BAC = 60°. Because △CDE is an equilateral triangle, CD = CE, and ∠DCE = 60°. Therefore ∠ACB = ∠DCE. Subtracting the common angle ∠BCE, we get ∠ACE = ∠BCD. Thus in △ACE and △BCD, AC = BC, CE = CD, and the included angle ∠ACE = ∠BCD, so △ACE ≅ △BCD (SAS). Therefore the corresponding angles ∠CAE = ∠CBD. In the figure, ∠EBD is composed of ∠EBC and ∠CBD, and ∠EBD = 50°, so ∠EBC + ∠CAE = 50°. Also because in △ABC, ∠CAB = ∠ABC = 60°, so ∠BAE + ∠ABE = (60° - ∠CAE) + (60° - ∠EBC) = 120° - 50° = 70°. In △AEB, ∠AEB = 180° - 70° = 110°.
